rv.q: But the writer doesn’t have a tight enough grip on all his threads, which also include Brexit, coronavirus and gender politics; nor are his characters fully realised enough to make the human interplay as compelling as the ideas.
It’s incredibly smart, but there’s not quite enough heart.

But in the end the play’s ambition defeats it: the improbable scenarios increasingly undermine the seriousness of the issues, the multiple questions raised are not deeply interrogated, the sketchy characterisation is both limiting and troubling.

Whatever the merits of Smith's play, we don't need over three hours to ponder them.

This is a show of half-finished thoughts and botched fixes.
But the Court still has an embarrassment on its hands: how did Al Smith’s shambolic, three-hour satire get staged in the first place?
Which is one of the dullest I have seen this year.

Smith’s play, running at over three hours, never feels it; instead, it is sprightly and often very witty as it dashes between these four perspectives as the players all try to outsmart and double-cross each other.
Rare Earth Mettle gets a very glitzy production but, while the shifting negotiations that make up the plot hold the attention, their results have to be imagined.
Indeed, Jewishness turns out to be entirely irrelevant to a baggy, shapeless but appealingly acted play that seems to have drawn attention for all the wrong reasons.
Ultimately though, Rare Earth Mettle is frustratingly hard to connect with and, in Pirie's uncompromisingly stark production, proves as dry as the salt flats on which it is mainly set.
After this bad start, and quite a jinxed series of previews, Rare Earth Mettle is even worse on stage than it was on the page.
Their toasty bite-sized treats are the only competent service this embarrassing dump provides.
Never has the importance of language and money been portrayed so piercingly on stage.
It’s entertaining, provocative and sometimes very funny.

Terrifically played by Arthur Darvill, Finn is the best thing about Hamish Pirie’s over-long production which overreaches for contemporary relevance by scooping up just about every hot topic in the news.

cn.t: Critics find this topical satire about lithium exploitation largely underwhelming, with most citing bland writing, cartoonish characters, and flat execution that fails to match its ambitious scope, though some praise its timely themes.
